Camp
KAMP
n. (rendering Hebrew machaneh, Greek parembolē)
From Latin campus, a field or level plain, whence the field on which an army pitches. The Hebrew machaneh is from chānâh, to encamp or pitch, and means both the act of pitching and the encampment itself. Because Israel spent forty years as a camp rather than a country, the word bears an unusual doctrinal load: the camp was at once a military formation, a city, and a sanctuary precinct, and its ordering was given by God down to the position of each standard.

Biblical Definition

The camp of Israel was a theological arrangement before it was a military one. Every tribe pitched in an appointed place, and the whole was oriented around one centre: “Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch” (Num 2:2). The tabernacle in the middle meant that the nation slept each night in concentric rings around the presence of God, and that presence made the whole encampment holy ground with practical consequences: “For the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee” (Deu 23:14). Sanitation, sexual purity, and the treatment of the dead were all regulated by that one fact. After the golden calf the arrangement was reversed in judgment, and the meeting-place was put outside: “And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp... And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle” (Exo 33:7). That reversal becomes the pattern of the cross, for Christ suffered outside the gate as the sin offering whose body was burned without the camp, and the summons follows: “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). The believer's position is settled by where Christ is, and He is outside — which means the safety of the religious establishment is the one place the Christian may not seek.

Webster 1828 Definition

The ground on which an army pitches its tents; the encampment itself with its ordered ranks; and in Scripture the camp of Israel arrayed about the tabernacle, made holy by God's walking in its midst, and the place outside it where Christ suffered.

CAMP, n. 1. The ground on which an army pitch their tents, whether for a night or a longer period.

2. The order or arrangement of tents, or of troops disposed for lodging; the encampment.

3. An army; the whole body of persons encamped; as, the camp of Israel numbered six hundred thousand.

4. In Scripture, the encampment of the Israelites in the wilderness, disposed in ordered ranks about the tabernacle. Num. 2.

5. Without the camp; outside the encampment, the place of the burning of the sin offering, and of the reproach of Christ. Heb. 13.

Key Scripture

Numbers 2:2 — "Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch."

Deuteronomy 23:14 — "For the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee."

Exodus 33:7 — "And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the congregation. And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle of the congregation, which was without the camp."

Hebrews 13:13 — "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."

Modern Corruption

The wilderness camp is treated as mere ancient hygiene, so that its holiness legislation is read as primitive taboo rather than as instruction in the nearness of a holy God, and the call to go forth without the camp is domesticated into mild nonconformity.

expand to see more

The regulations governing the camp — what must be buried, who must be put outside, what renders a man unclean until evening — are commonly explained as an ancient people's sanitary code, given a religious veneer. The text supplies its own reason and it is not hygiene: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp. The laws exist because God is present, and their purpose is that He see no unclean thing and not turn away. That reading is confirmed by the fact that many of the ordinances have no sanitary value whatever, and by the New Testament's treatment of them as shadows of a moral reality. To reduce them to public health is to miss the lesson the wilderness generation was being taught every day for forty years: that a holy God had moved in next door, and that this is a mercy and a danger at once.

The call of Heb 13:13 suffers a gentler corruption — it is quoted as a general encouragement to be a little countercultural, an endorsement of whatever nonconformity the reader already prefers. Its actual force is exact and costly. The camp in that passage is the whole apparatus of an established religion with divine credentials, temple, priesthood, and altar included; and the writer says Christ was put out of it and died there, so that His people must accept the same expulsion. The mark of the true church is therefore not respectability but a willingness to be located where Christ is, bearing his reproach, since here have we no continuing city. The principle to recover is that the reproach is not incidental to discipleship but is the address at which Christ may be found.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew machaneh is an encampment or army, from chānâh, to pitch or encamp; the same root gives place-names such as Mahanaim, the two camps. Greek parembolē is a camp, barracks, or army in array.

expand to see more

Hebrew machaneh (H4264) — camp, encampment, army; used of Israel in the wilderness and of the angelic host Jacob met (Gen 32:2).

Hebrew chānâh (H2583) — to pitch a tent, encamp, or lay siege; the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him (Psa 34:7).

Hebrew Mahanaim — two camps; the place where Jacob, meeting the host of God, named the site for the double encampment of angels and men.

Greek parembolē (G3925) — an encampment, barracks, or army in battle order; used of the castle in Acts and of the camp in Heb 13:11-13.

Greek exō tēs parembolēs — without the camp; the place of the burning of the sin offering and of Christ's suffering outside the gate.

Usage

"Of the ordered encampment about the tabernacle: every man... by his own standard... about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch (Num 2:2)."

"Of holiness required by God's presence: the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp... therefore shall thy camp be holy (Deu 23:14)."

"Of the believer's place with Christ: let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb 13:13)."
